claim: AS69 is a β-wrapin engineered to bind monomeric α-synuclein with high affinity.
source: To this end, we have engineered the β-wrapin AS69 to bind monomeric α-synuclein with high affinity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the structural model and binding data presented in Figure 1.

claim: AS69 reduced the self-interaction of α-synuclein in cultured cells.
source: In cultured cells, AS69 reduced the self-interaction of α-synuclein and formation of visible α-synuclein aggregates.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: AS69 reduced formation of visible α-synuclein aggregates in cultured cells.
source: In cultured cells, AS69 reduced the self-interaction of α-synuclein and formation of visible α-synuclein aggregates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data showing reduced particle formation in cells expressing AS69 (Figure 2e,f).

claim: AS69 reduced α-synuclein aggregates in flies.
source: In flies, AS69 reduced α-synuclein aggregates and the locomotor deficit resulting from α-synuclein expression in neuronal cells.
evidence: This is supported by the filter trap assay data from Drosophila melanogaster shown in Figure 3d,e.

claim: AS69 reduced the locomotor deficit resulting from α-synuclein expression in neuronal cells in flies.
source: In flies, AS69 reduced α-synuclein aggregates and the locomotor deficit resulting from α-synuclein expression in neuronal cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the climbing assay data in Drosophila melanogaster shown in Figure 3b.

claim: AS69 highly sub-stoichiometrically inhibited both primary and autocatalytic secondary nucleation processes in vitro.
source: In biophysical experiments in vitro, AS69 highly sub-stoichiometrically inhibited both primary and autocatalytic secondary nucleation processes, even in the presence of a large excess of monomer.
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data shown in Figures 6 and 9.

claim: AS69 inhibited nucleation processes even in the presence of a large excess of monomer.
source: In biophysical experiments in vitro, AS69 highly sub-stoichiometrically inhibited both primary and autocatalytic secondary nucleation processes, even in the presence of a large excess of monomer.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with high monomer:AS69 ratios shown in Figures 6 and 9.

claim: The AS69-α-synuclein complex, rather than the free AS69, is the inhibitory species responsible for sub-stoichiometric inhibition of secondary nucleation.
source: We present evidence that the AS69-α-synuclein complex, rather than the free AS69, is the inhibitory species responsible for sub-stoichiometric inhibition of secondary nucleation.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that the covalent AS69fusASN complex is equally effective as free AS69 (Figure 8).

claim: High affinity monomer binders can lead to strongly sub-stoichiometric inhibition of nucleation processes.
source: These results represent a new paradigm that high affinity monomer binders can lead to strongly sub-stoichiometric inhibition of nucleation processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing sub-stoichiometric inhibition by AS69.

claim: Introduction of a disulfide bond in the region comprising residues 37–54 strongly modulates α-synuclein aggregation.
source: Accordingly, modification of the local conformation by, for example, introduction of a disulfide bond strongly modulates aggregation (Shaykhalishahi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Shaykhalishahi et al., 2015.

claim: Co-expression of AS69 with both WT and A53T α-synuclein reduced the number and fraction of fluorescent cells in the BiFC assay.
source: Co-expression of AS69 with both variants reduced the number and fraction of fluorescent cells (Figure 2b, p<0.05 for WT and p<0.01 for A53T, two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2b with statistical analysis.

claim: Fibril elongation is inhibited by AS69 in a stoichiometric concentration-dependent manner.
source: The results indicate that fibril elongation is indeed inhibited by AS69 in a stoichiometric concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data and analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Fibrils formed in the presence of increasing concentrations of AS69 are morphologically indistinguishable from the fibrils formed in the absence of AS69.
source: This conclusion is supported by the finding that the fibrils formed in the presence of increasing concentrations of AS69 are morphologically indistinguishable from the fibrils formed in the absence of AS69 (as judged from AFM images, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the AFM images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AS69 does not show a preferential interaction with fibril ends.
source: Our kinetic analysis of fibril elongation in the presence of AS69 does not, however, suggest a preferential interaction with fibril ends, as such an interaction can be expected to lead to a sub-stoichiometric inhibition of fibril elongation, which is not observed in our experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from the stoichiometric nature of the inhibition observed in the elongation experiments.

claim: Density gradient centrifugation of samples containing only seeds and AS69 did not show AS69 to co-migrate with large species to any significant extent under conditions that favour elongation.
source: Furthermore, density gradient centrifugation (DGC) of samples containing only seeds and AS69 (Figure 5a and b) did not show AS69 to co-migrate with large species to any significant extent under conditions that favour elongation.
evidence: This is supported by the DGC data shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Under mildly acidic solution conditions with very low concentrations of pre-formed fibrils under quiescent conditions, seeded aggregation is inhibited by AS69 in a strongly sub-stoichiometric manner.
source: We find that under these solution conditions, where only growth and secondary nucleation contribute to the increase in fibril mass and number, respectively, the seeded aggregation is inhibited in a strongly sub-stoichiometric manner (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: Co-migration in the density gradient of AS69 with fibrils was undetectable under secondary nucleation-inducing solution conditions.
source: To investigate whether AS69 binds to the fibril surface under these secondary nucleation-inducing solution conditions, we performed additional DGC experiments. Co-migration in the density gradient of AS69 with fibrils, which would imply direct interactions between these species, was undetectable (Figure 7a–c).
evidence: This is supported by the DGC data shown in Figure 7a-c.

claim: The pre-formed AS69-α-synuclein complex is a similarly efficient inhibitor as the free AS69 under secondary nucleation conditions.
source: We found that the pre-formed complex is a similarly efficient inhibitor as the free AS69 under secondary nucleation conditions (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: The melting temperature of DMPS vesicles is decreased in the presence of AS69.
source: We find that the melting temperature of DMPS vesicles is decreased in the presence of AS69 (Figure 9—figure supplement 2a,b) and, furthermore, titration of AS69 into DMPS-SUV reveals a complex signature of heat release and consumption (Figure 9—figure supplement 2c,d).
evidence: This is supported by the DSC data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: Titration of AS69 into DMPS-SUV reveals a complex signature of heat release and consumption.
source: We find that the melting temperature of DMPS vesicles is decreased in the presence of AS69 (Figure 9—figure supplement 2a,b) and, furthermore, titration of AS69 into DMPS-SUV reveals a complex signature of heat release and consumption (Figure 9—figure supplement 2c,d).
evidence: This is supported by the ITC data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2c,d.

claim: There is a direct interaction between AS69 and DMPS-SUV.
source: While a detailed analysis of this interaction behaviour is beyond the scope of the present study, taken together these calorimetric experiments suggest indeed a direct interaction between AS69 and DMPS-SUV.
evidence: This is inferred from the DSC and ITC data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: AS69 represents a new paradigm in the inhibition of amyloid fibril formation: strongly sub-stoichiometric inhibition by a tight monomer-binding species.
source: Therefore, the AS69 affibody represents a new paradigm in the inhibition of amyloid fibril formation: strongly sub-stoichiometric inhibition by a tight monomer-binding species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing the unique mode of action of AS69.

claim: In the AS69 mode of action, it is not the inhibitor itself that plays the role of a molecular chaperone, but rather the monomer-inhibitor complex acts as a chaperone.
source: In this scenario, it is not the inhibitor itself that plays the role of a molecular chaperone, that is interacting with an on-pathway species and interfering with its further evolution, but rather the monomer-inhibitor complex acts as a chaperone.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental data showing that the AS69-α-synuclein complex is the inhibitory species.

claim: Under mildly acidic solution conditions with very low concentrations of pre-formed fibrils under quiescent conditions, seeded aggregation consists of fibril elongation, secondary nucleation, and higher order assembly.
source: Under those solution conditions, seeded aggregation has been shown to consist of two processes in addition to fibril elongation, namely secondary nucleation, which increases the number of growth competent fibril ends, and higher order assembly ('flocculation', Figure 6—figure supplement 1b,c), which decreases the overall aggregation rate by reducing the number of accessible fibrils through their burial within higher order aggregates (Buell et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Buell et al., 2014a.

claim: Secondary nucleation increases the number of growth competent fibril ends.
source: Under those solution conditions, seeded aggregation has been shown to consist of two processes in addition to fibril elongation, namely secondary nucleation, which increases the number of growth competent fibril ends, and higher order assembly ('flocculation', Figure 6—figure supplement 1b,c), which decreases the overall aggregation rate by reducing the number of accessible fibrils through their burial within higher order aggregates (Buell et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is a mechanistic description supported by the citation to Buell et al., 2014a.

claim: Higher order assembly decreases the overall aggregation rate by reducing the number of accessible fibrils through their burial within higher order aggregates.
source: Under those solution conditions, seeded aggregation has been shown to consist of two processes in addition to fibril elongation, namely secondary nucleation, which increases the number of growth competent fibril ends, and higher order assembly ('flocculation', Figure 6—figure supplement 1b,c), which decreases the overall aggregation rate by reducing the number of accessible fibrils through their burial within higher order aggregates (Buell et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is a mechanistic description supported by the citation to Buell et al., 2014a.

claim: The de novo formation of amyloid fibrils through primary nucleation is suppressed if the solution is not agitated and if non-binding surfaces are used.
source: The de novo formation of amyloid fibrils through primary nucleation is suppressed if the solution is not agitated and if non-binding surfaces are used (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The absence of detectable binding of AS69 to fibrils in DGC experiments implies either a weak affinity for fibrils or a very low stoichiometry.
source: Therefore, the absence of detectable binding implies either a weak affinity for fibrils or a very low stoichiometry, that is a very low density of binding sites for AS69 on the fibril surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the DGC data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The difference in melting temperatures between the covalent and non-covalent AS69-α-synuclein complex can be explained by the differences in the entropy of binding.
source: The difference in melting temperatures between the covalent and non-covalent complex can be explained by the differences in the entropy of binding, which is more unfavourable in the case of the non-covalent complex, given the loss of three degrees of freedom of translational motion upon binding.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic interpretation of the observed difference in melting temperatures.

claim: AS69 is a very efficient inhibitor of secondary nucleation at highly sub-stoichiometric ratios.
source: Second, AS69 is found to be a very efficient inhibitor of secondary nucleation at highly sub-stoichiometric ratios.
evidence: This is supported by the secondary nucleation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The inhibitory effect of AS69 on secondary nucleation is unlikely to stem from a direct interaction between the AS69 and either fibril surfaces or secondary nucleation intermediates.
source: The overall result of our experimental and theoretical analysis is that this inhibitory effect is unlikely to stem from a direct interaction between the AS69 and either fibril surfaces or secondary nucleation intermediates.
evidence: This is inferred from the DGC data, MST data, and theoretical analysis.

claim: The AS69 affibody represents a new paradigm: strongly sub-stoichiometric inhibition by a tight monomer-binding species.
source: Therefore, the AS69 affibody represents a new paradigm in the inhibition of amyloid fibril formation: strongly sub-stoichiometric inhibition by a tight monomer-binding species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unique mode of action demonstrated by the experimental data.

claim: Molecular chaperones exhibit sub-stoichiometric inhibitory behaviour but do not interact significantly with the monomer.
source: In the case of molecular chaperones, on the other hand, sub-stoichiometric inhibitory behaviour has been reported previously (Waudby et al., 2010; Månsson et al., 2014), but it is usually found that these molecules do not interact significantly with the monomer, but rather bind specifically to aggregated states of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Waudby et al., 2010 and Månsson et al., 2014.

claim: It is straightforward to develop molecules that bind to the monomeric forms of proteins.
source: First, it is rather straightforward to develop further molecules that bind to the monomeric forms of proteins, given that the latter are well-defined, reproducible and easy to handle.
evidence: This is a general statement about protein engineering based on established knowledge.

claim: Targeting on-pathway aggregation intermediates is difficult because they are difficult to isolate for the development of inhibitors.
source: This simplicity is in contrast to the difficulty presented by targeting on-pathway aggregation intermediates which are difficult to isolate for the development of inhibitors.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenges in targeting aggregation intermediates based on established knowledge.

claim: Binders of oligomeric aggregation intermediates can be expected to be less specific compared to binders of a well-defined monomeric state.
source: Second, binders of oligomeric aggregation intermediates can be expected to be less specific compared to binders of a well-defined monomeric state, as suggested by the existence of antibodies that interact with protofibrillar species independently of the protein from which they have formed (Kayed et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Kayed et al., 2003.

claim: The mode of inhibition presented by AS69 avoids the need for stoichiometric amounts of inhibitors that are usually required in the case of monomer-sequestering species.
source: And third, the mode of inhibition presented here avoids the need for stoichiometric amounts of inhibitors that are usually required in the case of monomer-sequestering species, resulting in a more efficient inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the sub-stoichiometric inhibition data.

claim: High affinity monomer binders displaying strong sub-stoichiometric inhibition of fibril formation represent attractive agents to interfere with pathological protein aggregation.
source: In conclusion, high affinity monomer binders displaying strong sub-stoichiometric inhibition of fibril formation represent attractive agents to interfere with pathological protein aggregation, as a result of their multiple inhibitory action.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: AS69 is a disulfide-linked homodimer.
source: AS69 (grey) is a disulfide-linked homodimer.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1a and shown in the structural model.

claim: Under conditions of vigorous shaking, primary nucleation can occur readily at the air-water interface.
source: With vigorous shaking, for instance, primary nucleation can occur readily at the air-water interface (Campioni et al., 2014) and fibril fragmentation induced by the shaking amplifies the number of growth-competent fibril ends (Xue et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Campioni et al., 2014.

claim: Fibril fragmentation induced by shaking amplifies the number of growth-competent fibril ends.
source: With vigorous shaking, for instance, primary nucleation can occur readily at the air-water interface (Campioni et al., 2014) and fibril fragmentation induced by the shaking amplifies the number of growth-competent fibril ends (Xue et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Xue et al., 2009.
